```console
\subsection{A leaderboard with missing cells}\label{sec:sparse}
The leaderboard an evaluator holds has missing cells, so we repeat the protocol on MTEB matrices with their real gaps: English tasks reported for at least 20 models (445 models $\times$ 335 tasks, 21\% of cells observed) and English and all-task subsets trimmed to 30, 50 and 70\% observed (Table~\ref{tab:sparse}; construction in Appendix~\ref{app:sparse}). A test model is a model with at least 30 observed cells, held out by family as before; its observed cells are split at random into 30\% targets and 70\% candidates, and $k$ benchmarks are chosen among the candidates. The factor model is fitted by masked EM on the training models; as a second predictor we use the pairwise-complete correlation matrix, shrunk toward the identity (``pw''); the LOBO reference conditions on all candidates, with the better of the two predictors, so closure can exceed 1.
Greedy A beats random selection at every $k=1,\dots,20$ on every subset, for both predictors (the interval excludes zero in all cells but one: pw at $k=20$ on the 21\% subset). At $k=3$ the gap is 5--7\% of the random error with pw, and 6--24\% with the factor model, whose random selections are poor on the all-task subsets. Greedy A closes 0.71--0.80 of the gap to LOBO at $k=3$ (pw), random selection 0.55--0.74; the level 0.9 is reached by greedy A at $k=6$ to 20, with wide intervals (the widest $[3,>20]$ on the 21\% subset), and by random selection later or not within 20 (Table~\ref{tab:sparse}). Between 30 and 70\% observed cells the results change little. They are not shown for densities below 21\%, for models with fewer than 30 observed cells, for the logit transform (identity only), or beyond $k=20$, and their RMSE is not comparable with the dense pools (each model is scored on its own random observed cells). The dense pools remain the controlled experiment.
Selection also tolerates a smaller dense history, but not missingness that concentrates on weaker models (Appendix~\ref{app:history}).
\subsection{Sparse leaderboard matrix}\label{app:sparse}
The six subsets keep the real missing cells of the MTEB score matrix. \emph{English, 21\%} holds the 445 models and 335 English tasks reported for at least 20 models (a median of 60 observed cells per model; 337 models have at least 30). The other subsets are greedy trimmings of the English tasks (332$\times$295, 268$\times$176 and 226$\times$134 at 30, 50 and 70\% observed) and of all tasks (331$\times$705 and 236$\times$517 at 30 and 50\%); the trimmed subsets are one greedy choice among many. Models are grouped by family and held out in ten folds as in the dense pools. A training column needs at least 10 observed training cells and is standardised on its observed training cells; only the identity transform is used. A model with at least 30 observed cells is a test model; for each of three random partitions, 30\% of its observed cells (rounded) are the targets and the remaining cells are the candidates, from which the selector chooses; the predictor uses only the selected cells. Greedy A uses the masked-EM factor-model covariance; random selection averages 30 draws per $k$ (the dense runs average 50 to 200). The factor model chooses its rank by five-fold held-out masked marginal likelihood and the one-standard-error rule. The pairwise predictor takes pairwise-complete correlations, clips them to a positive semi-definite matrix and shrinks them toward the identity, with the shrinkage in $\{0.02,\dots,0.4\}$ chosen on training rows. A masked Soft-Impute fold-in is only slightly better than the column mean (its fold-in shrinks the cells it cannot see) and is omitted from Table~\ref{tab:sparse}. Standardised RMSE is the square root of the mean over test models of the per-model mean squared error.
